comments.text: One of the things Botswana had that a lot of post-colonial nations in Africa didn't have, was a sense of continuity in its governance. Botswana was a fairly 'hands-off' British protectorate which meant that many of its traditional community assemblies and local institutions were able to remain intact both before and after independence. It also helped that the government realized early on that they needed to have a government stake in the diamond trade so that all of that wealth wouldn't be siphoned out of the country.

comments.author: @susettehorspool2646
comments.text: I was a Peace Corps volunteer there in 1974-76 and don't remember hearing anything about diamonds. Copper, yes, and I was part of the project to introduce cattle production as a national industry to the villagers (now Botswana's 3rd biggest industry). I also had buddies who helped the government decide whether to divert water from the Okavango Swamps for agriculture (they didn't) or to preserve it to expand the tourist safari industry (now Botswana's 4th biggest industry). I can see that leadership were excited about discovering diamonds, but they cared more about creating a stable, balanced economy, rather than going all out after that single, sure source of riches. I met Sir Seretse Khama and respect him highly.

replies.author: @susettehorspool2646
replies.text: Also, I heard that Sir Seretse gave up his chieftainship as a condition of taking over as President of Botswana, and that the chiefs of both other major tribes were given influential roles in the new government. Sir Seretse's wife did right by the country and was highly revered by the time I got there 8 years after independence.

replies.author: @susettehorspool2646
